title: Cluny
hookLine: a reforming monastery whose monks prayed almost without stopping

lines: A DUKE GIVES AWAY HIS LAND.
cards: A duke sits down to give away a piece of his own land. His name is William, and the land is a place called Cluny, in Burgundy. In the charter he signs, he doesn't hand it to a bishop or a king.
He gives it to the apostles Peter and Paul, for a house of monks. Then he adds something unusual. Nobody, not his own heirs, not a prince, not even a bishop, is to interfere with them.
The monks will choose their own abbot. Why would a powerful man tie his own hands like that? Because he wanted one thing done there, without interruption, for good.

teach.b: The thing done at Cluny was prayer. The charter places its monks under the Rule of Saint Benedict, which sets prayer at fixed hours through the day and the night, and says nothing is to be put before the work of God.
The Rule leans on a line from the Psalms, in the King James words: "Seven times a day do I praise thee."
Cluny took that and kept going. Its monks are remembered for adding psalms, processions and long prayers for the dead, until the singing in the church seemed hardly to stop.
Behind it sits a short line from Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians, in the King James wording: "Pray without ceasing." Christians have read that line in more than one way.

teach.h: A SCHEDULE, A BREATH, A POSTURE.
teach.b: Some, like the Cluny monks, read it as a schedule: build a life where the prayer never stops, because someone is always at it.

Some Orthodox Christians read it as a prayer carried inward, a short line repeated until it travels with the breath. Some Protestants hear it as a posture: a whole day turned toward God, at the sink and on the bus.
The readings don't cancel each other. And Cluny's way spread. Tradition remembers other monasteries asking to be reformed by it and joining its family of houses.
Later critics, as this path will see, thought it grew too rich. But at its heart was a simple, stubborn idea: somewhere, someone should always be praying.

how: Monks and nuns in Benedictine communities still gather at set hours of the day and night to sing the psalms, and some Christians outside monasteries pray shorter forms of those hours in the morning and evening.

games.q: you're a duke giving land for a monastery, and you want its prayer to last. what do you write into the charter?
o: put it under your own family, to protect it.
put it under the local bishop.
give it to the apostles and forbid anyone to interfere.
games.why: William gives Cluny to Peter and Paul and bars his heirs, princes and even bishops from interfering. the monks choose their own abbot, so nothing interrupts the prayer.

practice: If you pray, pray the way you usually do, and when you reach the place where you'd normally stop, stay a little more, repeating a line you already know or keeping company in silence.
If you don't pray, sit with your breath, and when the urge to get up arrives, notice it, and stay anyway. At Cluny, one psalm led into the next.

wordCard.voice: Cluny. A monastery in Burgundy, given to the apostles and left free, where the monks' prayer seemed never to stop.

orig.note: Greek: unceasingly — the word Paul uses in 1 Thessalonians 5:17.
